TrueFoundry is an AI infrastructure company headquartered in San Francisco, building the production layer for AI agents. Its flagship open-source product, TrueForge , provides teams with everything needed to build, deploy, debug, and govern production-grade AI agents — supporting any model and any MCP server within their own infrastructure. Enterprises including NetApp are already using TrueFoundry to run production agents at scale.

business_outcome: Cost optimization : Total agent operating costs reduced by approximately 50% compared to managed, single-vendor agent platforms. Widest open coverage : Qwen's model spectrum — from sub-billion to 480B parameters — gives TrueForge users access to the most comprehensive selection of open models behind a single API. Zero-integration switching : Moving between model sizes is frictionless — no code rewrites or re-integrations required, making right-sizing a natural habit. Unified governance : One API, one dashboard, one budget — observability and spend caps apply consistently across every model size.
architecture_clues: TrueFoundry chose Alibaba's Qwen as a founding model partner for TrueForge's open-source launch, driven by several key factors:

Broadest open-model spectrum : Qwen offers the widest range of open models of any AI lab — from sub-billion-parameter models to the flagship Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B with up to one-million-token context on coding models
Family coherence : All Qwen models share a unified family identity and function-call format, so switching between sizes feels seamless rather than like integrating a new provider
Production-grade capabilities : The Qwen coding line achieves state-of-the-art results among open models on agentic coding and tool-use tasks, performing on par with leading closed models
Open-weight philosophy : Qwen's open-weight approach aligns with TrueFoundry's vendor-neutral ethos
Teams can deploy Qwen models on their own infrastructure without proprietary restrictions
evidence_quotes: As the AI agent ecosystem matured, TrueFoundry identified four critical barriers teams face when moving from prototype to production:
Model fragmentation : Not every agent task requires the largest model.
A quick file edit does not justify a frontier-scale invocation, and a repository-wide refactor demands the most capable model available.
Most teams need both, but stitching together separate providers creates significant integration overhead.
Vendor lock-in : Most managed agent platforms address production complexity by locking teams into a single model provider.
